analysis.one_liner: Requires people earning over $1 million a year to pay at least 30% of their income in federal taxes.
analysis.headline: A bill to require millionaires to pay at least 30% income tax died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, vote, or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a new minimum tax: anyone whose adjusted gross income tops $1 million would pay at least 30% of that income in federal taxes, whatever mix of salary, investments, and deductions they used. It would only apply to the amount above what someone already owes in income and payroll taxes, and the $1 million threshold would rise with inflation. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and stayed there until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the chief beneficiaries would be everyone else who pays taxes: the bill's supporters estimate a 30% floor on million-dollar incomes would raise billions of dollars a year, reducing deficits or funding priorities without touching households under $1 million [S3]. It would also blunt the advantage that very high earners get from capital-gains rates, loopholes, and deductions that let some pay effective rates well below 30%.

how_it_helps.text: It imposes a minimum 30% tax rate on adjusted gross income above $1 million, so taxpayers in that bracket can no longer pay a lower effective rate than middle-income earners.
The tax is the excess of the 30% minimum over what the taxpayer already owes in regular tax, alternative minimum tax, and payroll tax, so it only raises bills for those currently paying below 30%.
The $1 million threshold is adjusted for inflation after 2023, so the tax stays aimed at the top rather than drifting down the income scale.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall entirely on taxpayers with adjusted gross income above $1 million, roughly the top fraction of one percent of filers, who would owe additional tax whenever their effective rate fell below 30%. High earners with sophisticated tax planning would lose the most, since the minimum tax overrides many strategies for reducing taxable income.

drawbacks.text: A parallel minimum tax layered on top of the existing income tax and AMT adds a third set of rules, making the tax code more complex for high earners and for the IRS to administer.

Critics of minimum-tax approaches argue that taxing adjusted gross income rather than realized gains can pressure high earners to restructure income or defer realizing gains, and that the bill does not itself close the loopholes it calls out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a meaningful revenue gain from a very small group that can most afford it, with deductions preserved for charitable giving and credits. The cost is added complexity to an already complicated tax code and a possible incentive for high earners to shift or defer income; some economists prefer closing loopholes directly over layering on a parallel minimum tax. The bill's own sense-of-the-Senate section concedes it is an "interim step" rather than the fundamental simplification supporters say is needed [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on April 18, 2023, joined by 15 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats [S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance; that referral is the last entry in its action history [S5].
The Finance Committee never held a markup or vote on the bill, and the full Senate never debated it; the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with incomes above $1 million, who will continue paying effective tax rates below 30% because the bill never advanced; the Finance Committee also kept its agenda unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 18, 2023, to impose a 30% minimum tax on incomes over $1 million.

for.name: 15 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Sanders, Warren, Klobuchar, and Durbin; no Republican cosponsored.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred; it died there.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Minority in the Senate, majority on the Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Senate's 60-vote supermajority rule meant majority-only support could not overcome a filibuster; the bill never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republicans signed on, and the bill died in committee without floor action [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Households earning over $1 million per year
industries.note: The bill sets a 30% floor on the effective tax rate for million-dollar earners, who currently use deductions and preferential rates to pay less [S2][S3]. It is the concentrated interest the bill exists to tax.

industries.industry: Tax advisory and wealth management services
industries.note: A minimum tax reduces the payoff from sophisticated tax planning, though demand for advice would persist under any code.
Charitable contributions remain deductible under the minimum tax, but only proportionally for itemizers, which could modestly change giving incentives at the top.
